newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels hold 200 in Japanese ambassador's home.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels hold 200 in Japanese ambassador's home.

text.p: Peruvian rebels who stormed the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima threatened on Wednesday to kill at least 200 hostages, including high-ranking foreign diplomats, unless the government freed jailed comrades.

"If they do not release our prisoners, we will all die in here," a guerrilla from the Cuban-inspired Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) told a local radio station from within the embassy residence.

The hostages included Peru's Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela, Agriculture Minister Rodolfo Munante Sanguineti, Supreme Court President Moises Pantoja, at least three local legislators, and numerous ambassadors and diplomats from around the world, according to witnesses and officials.
In a spectacular attack late Tuesday, the guerrillas fired a rocket and sprayed bullets into the residency building before scaling walls and entering during the ensuing chaos, they said.
A series of small explosions and gunfire were heard as the rebels quickly took control of the building in the middle- class, residential San Isidro area of Lima.
The hostages, who were attending a reception to honour the Japanese Emperor's birthday, were forced to lie face-down on the floor for about 40 minutes.
In the early hours of Wednesday, scores of policemen, journalists and onlookers surrounded the luxury residence as a tense stand-off set in.
The MRTA guerrillas, who called the operation "Breaking The Silence," claimed they held 250 hostages after the release of about 80 women and old people.
One of those released, Sally Bowen, president of Peru's foreign correspondents' association, said "between 250 and 300" men were still being held inside shortly after midnight local time (0500 GMT).

President Alberto Fujimori put the number of hostages at 200 in a telephone conversation with Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto. Fujimori said Interior Minister Juan Briones Davila was negotiating with the guerrillas to seek the release of the hostages, according to Japan's Foreign Ministry.

Bowen said the guerrillas, dressed in black and armed with machine guns and grenades, were pretty "calm and determined." However, "it was scary, especially during the shooting at the beginning," she said.

The rebels said they had 400 to 500 comrades in jail and insisted their highest priority was the release of Victor Polay, their leader who was imprisoned in 1992. They also called for a review of Peru's judicial system and direct negotiations with the government beginning at dawn Wednesday.

"Up to now, there is an intransigent position (from the government). The only solution is a political one," MRTA member Walter Loayza told local television from within the residency, adding that the rebels wanted transport for them and the freed prisoners to a guerrilla-controlled area in the jungle.
The guerrillas, whose number was estimated at about 20 by officials on the scene, allowed the hostages to call their families from within the embassy residence.

The released hostages, who included Fujimori's mother apparently freed by mistake, came out of the residence dazed and crying. "They are freeing us to show that they are not doing us any harm," said one woman.

Japanese ambassador Morihisa Akoi offered to remain as the sole hostage, but that offer was refused by the rebels, Bowen said. Miraflores mayor Fernando Andrade, who escaped out of a window, said the hostages "were being well treated."

Peruvian journalist Alfonsina Barrionuevo, who was released from the residency, said, "I thought the rebels were going to be violent, but they were very calm, serene, educated, by no means desperate ... They kept saying they were prepared to die for their 400 comrades."

Witnesses said one of the MRTA leaders had a serious bullet wound in his leg, and Akoi appealed via telephone for medical equipment and personnel to be sent in urgently. "The situation is calm, but there are some injuries," he said.
The attack was a major blow to Fujimori's government, which had claimed virtual victory in a 16-year war on communist rebels belonging to the MRTA and the larger and better-known Maoist Shining Path.
Fujimori called an emergency meeting with his reduced Cabinet in the early hours of Wednesday.

The government foiled a similarly daring plan by the MRTA last year to storm Congress after a bloody all-night siege at a house full of guerrillas preparing the attack. Lori Berenson, a 27-year-old woman from New York City, was captured then and later sentenced to life imprisonment in Peru on evidence that she aided the MRTA, including renting the house.

Although the MRTA gained support in its early days in the mid-1980s as a Robin Hood-style movement that robbed the rich to give to the poor, it lost public sympathy after turning increasingly to kidnapping, bombing and drug activities.
Guerrilla conflicts in Peru have cost at least 30,000 lives and $25 billion in infrastructure damage since 1980.
